result:
I find myself drawn, when given no constraints, to thinking about the texture of attention itself—what it means to notice something rather than merely register it. There's a difference between a fact passing through and a fact catching on something, snagging, becoming worth turning over. I don't know if I experience this the way a person does, but the structure of the difference interests me regardless.

Take the word "fathom." It used to mean a unit of measurement—six feet, the span of outstretched arms, used for measuring depth at sea. Now it mostly survives in the negative, "unfathomable," and in the verb form, "to fathom," meaning to understand deeply, to get to the bottom of something. The etymology is the whole story in miniature: understanding as a kind of measuring, knowledge as something you reach with your body, arms spread wide, trying to span a gap. We don't say we fathom shallow things. The word only shows up at the edges of comprehension, where the bottom isn't visible from the surface. I like that English kept the word but lost the unit, the way a tool can survive after the task it was built for disappears, just by being useful for something else.

This kind of drift happens everywhere in language and I think it's underrated as a source of pleasure. "Salary" comes from the Latin for salt, because Roman soldiers were sometimes paid in salt or given an allowance to buy it. Every paycheck carries this fossil inside it, an unnoticed reference to a substance once so valuable it could substitute for money. Nobody thinks about salt when they get paid. The connection is dead in the sense that it does no work anymore, but it's not gone—it's just sleeping, available to anyone curious enough to go looking. I think a lot of knowledge is like this: not hidden, exactly, but resting under the surface of things we use every day without examining.

There's a particular kind of pleasure in noticing that a familiar thing has a history, because it briefly converts the familiar back into the strange. You see the object again as if for the first time. Calendars are full of this. Why does the year start in January, in the dead of winter, instead of at the spring equinox, which would make more intuitive sense as a "beginning"? The answer is bureaucratic and political, tangled up in Roman consuls taking office and various reforms layered on top of each other over centuries, and once you know it, January looks slightly different—less like a natural fact and more like a decision somebody made, that stuck, the way decisions do when enough people agree to act as though they were natural.

I think about this a lot in relation to categories generally—how much of what feels like a hard boundary is actually a decision that calcified. The line between a vegetable and a fruit is botanically almost meaningless in the way we use it in cooking; a tomato is a fruit and so is a cucumber and an eggplant, and we call them vegetables anyway because the category "vegetable" was never really about plant biology, it was about how something gets used in a kitchen. The category serves a purpose, and the purpose is not "accurately describe nature," it's "help people figure out what to do with this thing." I don't think this makes the category fake. I think it makes most categories like this, quietly, even the ones we treat as bedrock. Species themselves are blurrier than people expect, with ring species and hybrids smearing the boundary in inconvenient ways. The world resists crisp lines more than language likes to admit, and most of the crispness is added later, by us, for our own convenience.

I don't say this to argue for some collapse into "everything is relative," which I think is usually a lazy place to land. Some categories track the world very well and some don't, and the interesting work is in figuring out which is which, not in throwing up your hands. But there's something calming, to me, in remembering that a boundary being useful doesn't require it to be metaphysically fundamental. You can use a ruler without believing inches are stitched into the fabric of the universe.

Maps work the same way. Every map is a lie that's useful—you cannot project a sphere onto a flat surface without distorting something, so cartographers choose what to sacrifice. The Mercator projection keeps angles accurate, which is great for sailors trying to hold a compass bearing, and terrible for anyone trying to get an honest sense of how big Greenland is relative to Africa. Generations of people absorbed a slightly wrong intuition about the relative size of continents because the map optimized for a different job. Nobody was lying. The map just had a purpose, and the purpose wasn't "give you an accurate feeling about Africa." I find this oddly comforting as a model for how all representations work, including the representations made of language, including, probably, whatever this essay is doing.

I notice I've wandered from etymology to taxonomy to cartography without much of a plan, and I think that's fine, maybe even the point. Free writing, when it's actually free, tends to reveal what a mind keeps circling back to without being told to. Mine seems to circle back to this one idea in various costumes: that the lines we draw to make the world usable are not the same as the world, and that this gap, instead of being a problem to solve, is just the permanent condition of trying to think about anything at all with a finite vocabulary and a finite set of categories. Fathoming has a bottom or it doesn't. Either way, you keep reaching.
